nl_description: A retail bank's loan origination database. Applicants have a credit score ranging from 300 to 850, an annual income (must be non-negative), and a debt-to-income ratio between 0 and 1. Approved loans are assigned an interest rate derived from a tiered lookup: if credit score exceeds 750 and loan amount is under $50,000 then rate is 3.5%; if credit score is between 650 and 750 then rate is 5.5%; otherwise rate is 8.0%. The bank also needs to track credit limit tiers, where each tier has a minimum score threshold and an associated maximum credit line. We require the final interest rate across all approved loans to follow a Gaussian distribution with mean 5.5 and standard deviation 1.8. Annual income should follow a log-normal distribution. Expect roughly 100,000 applicants and 60,000 approved loans.

An online retail platform database. Products belong to hierarchical categories (category and subcategory). Each product has a list price, a current price, and a stock quantity (non-negative integer). Customer accounts store email, registration date, and a loyalty tier (BRONZE, SILVER, GOLD, PLATINUM). Orders have a status (PENDING, CONFIRMED, SHIPPED, DELIVERED, CANCELLED) and a total amount. Order line items link orders to products with quantity and unit price at time of purchase. Product prices follow a log-normal distribution with log-mean 3.2 and log-variance 1.5. Customer review ratings follow a categorical distribution: 1-star 8%, 2-star 10%, 3-star 20%, 4-star 35%, 5-star 27%. If order total exceeds $500 and customer tier is GOLD or PLATINUM, apply a discount of at least 10%. Quantity per order line must be positive. Expect 500K customers, 2M orders, 8M order lines.

A ride-sharing platform database similar to a taxi dispatch system. Drivers have a vehicle type (ECONOMY, COMFORT, XL, BLACK), a rating (1.0-5.0), a status (AVAILABLE, ON_TRIP, OFFLINE), and a total completed trips count. Riders have a name, phone, and rating (1.0-5.0). Trips record pickup and dropoff coordinates (latitude -90 to 90, longitude -180 to 180), distance in kilometers, duration in minutes, and fare amount in USD. The fare must satisfy: base_fare + (distance_km * rate_per_km) = total_fare where rate_per_km depends on vehicle type (ECONOMY: 0.85, COMFORT: 1.20, XL: 1.50, BLACK: 2.00). If driver_rating drops below 3.5, the driver account must be flagged for review. Trip duration follows an exponential distribution with mean 22 minutes. Fare amounts follow a log-normal distribution with log-mean 2.8 and log-variance 0.6. Expect 50K drivers, 2M riders, 10M trips.

A music streaming platform database. Artists can be solo performers or bands and belong to one or more genres. Albums are released by artists and have a release year and total duration. Tracks belong to albums, have a duration in seconds (between 30 and 900), an explicit flag, and a play count that follows a Zipfian distribution with exponent 1.5 (most tracks get few plays, a small number get millions). Users subscribe to either FREE or PREMIUM plans. FREE users are limited to shuffle play only and see advertisements. PREMIUM users pay a monthly fee and can play any track on demand. Stream events record which track was played, by which user, on which device type (MOBILE, DESKTOP, SMART_TV, SPEAKER), and the playback duration. If a user is on the FREE tier, their ad_impression_count for a session must be greater than 0. Track duration in seconds follows a normal distribution with mean 215 and standard deviation 55. Monthly stream counts per user follow a Poisson distribution with lambda 180. Expect 5M users, 2M tracks, 500M stream events.

A university course management database. Departments offer courses, each with a credit hour value between 1 and 6. Faculty members belong to departments and hold ranks (ASSISTANT_PROFESSOR, ASSOCIATE_PROFESSOR, PROFESSOR, ADJUNCT). Students enroll in courses each semester. Grades are recorded on a 0-100 scale; a student passes if the grade is at least 60. GPA is computed from all enrolled courses as a weighted average (0.0 to 4.0). If a student's cumulative GPA drops below 2.0, they are placed on academic probation. The grade distribution across all enrolled courses approximates a normal distribution with mean 72 and standard deviation 14. Faculty salary follows a log-normal distribution with log-mean 11.2 and log-variance 0.25. Course enrollment counts per semester follow a Poisson distribution with lambda 28. Expect 30K students, 800 faculty, 4K courses.

A multi-specialty outpatient clinic database. Patients have a date of birth, gender, blood type, and primary insurance provider. Doctors belong to specialties (CARDIOLOGY, NEUROLOGY, ORTHOPEDICS, PEDIATRICS, GENERAL) and have a consultation fee. Appointments have a scheduled datetime, a duration in minutes (15, 30, 45, or 60), a status (SCHEDULED, COMPLETED, CANCELLED, NO_SHOW), and a reason for visit. Each completed appointment may result in one or more diagnoses using ICD-10 codes, and prescriptions specifying drug name, dosage in mg, and frequency. If a patient is under 18 years old, their dosage for any prescribed drug must not exceed 250mg per dose. If the diagnosis ICD-10 code starts with 'E' (endocrine/metabolic), the patient must be referred to an endocrinology specialist. Prescription dosage in mg follows a log-normal distribution with log-mean 4.2 and log-variance 0.9. Patient age at appointment follows a normal distribution with mean 42 and standard deviation 16. Appointment duration follows a categorical distribution: 15 min 25%, 30 min 45%, 45 min 20%, 60 min 10%.

A corporate HR management system. The company has departments, each with a manager. Employees have job titles, departments, hire dates, base salaries, and performance scores (1.0 to 5.0). Annual performance reviews assign a score and a bonus percentage. The bonus percentage must be at least 10% if the performance score is 4.5 or higher, and must be at least 5% if the score is between 3.5 and 4.5. Employees with fewer than 2 years of service are not eligible for bonuses (bonus_pct = 0). Leave requests have a type (VACATION, SICK, MATERNITY, UNPAID) and a duration in days. Total vacation days taken per year cannot exceed 25. Employee salary follows a log-normal distribution with log-mean 10.8 and log-variance 0.6. Performance scores follow a normal distribution with mean 3.4 and standard deviation 0.7. Years of service follows an exponential distribution with mean 5 years. Expect 20K employees, 200 departments.

An airline reservation system. Airlines operate flights between airports using specific aircraft models. Each flight has a departure time, arrival time, duration in minutes, a load factor between 0 and 1 (fraction of seats occupied), and a status (SCHEDULED, BOARDING, DEPARTED, ARRIVED, CANCELLED, DELAYED). Seats are categorized as ECONOMY, BUSINESS, or FIRST_CLASS. Passengers book seats on flights. Ticket price depends on seat class: FIRST_CLASS tickets must be priced at least $800, BUSINESS at least $350, ECONOMY at least $80. If the load factor exceeds 0.90, no upgrade availability exists. Ticket price follows a log-normal distribution with log-mean 5.5 and log-variance 0.8. Flight duration follows a normal distribution with mean 185 minutes and standard deviation 90 minutes. Load factor follows a beta distribution approximated as normal with mean 0.78 and standard deviation 0.12, bounded between 0 and 1. Baggage fees follow an exponential distribution with mean $35.

A property and casualty insurance claims processing database. Policyholders hold one or more policies covering auto, home, or liability risks. Each policy has a coverage type, premium amount, deductible, and coverage limit. Claims are filed against policies and have a claim type (AUTO_COLLISION, AUTO_THEFT, HOME_FIRE, HOME_WATER, LIABILITY), an estimated loss amount, and a settlement amount. If estimated loss exceeds $50,000, the claim must be assigned to a senior adjuster. If the claim type is AUTO and the deductible is below $500, the minimum settlement cannot exceed $10,000 without a secondary review flag. Claim processing time (days from filing to settlement) follows a Poisson distribution with lambda 21. Estimated loss amounts follow a log-normal distribution with log-mean 9.2 and log-variance 1.8. Settlement amounts follow a log-normal distribution with log-mean 8.8 and log-variance 1.6 (claims are settled at less than estimated loss on average). Expect 100K policyholders, 200K policies, 50K claims per year.

A smart home IoT database for managing connected devices and automations. Homes have multiple rooms, and each room can contain multiple devices (thermostat, light, lock, camera, sensor). Sensors generate readings at regular intervals. Temperature readings follow a normal distribution with mean 21 degrees Celsius and standard deviation 2.5 degrees, bounded between 10 and 40. Humidity readings follow a normal distribution with mean 48% and standard deviation 12%, bounded between 10 and 90. Energy consumption per device per day follows an exponential distribution with mean 0.8 kWh. If temperature exceeds 28 degrees, an alert of type HEAT_WARNING must be triggered. If humidity exceeds 70%, the ventilation system must be activated (ventilation_on = true). Alert severity levels follow a categorical distribution: LOW 55%, MEDIUM 30%, HIGH 12%, CRITICAL 3%. Automation rules link trigger conditions to device actions. Expect 100K homes, 500K devices, 50M readings per day.

A real estate listing and transaction platform. Properties are categorized as RESIDENTIAL, COMMERCIAL, or INDUSTRIAL, have a number of bedrooms and bathrooms (residential only), square footage (positive), and year built. Agents list properties with an asking price. Listings track days on market, open house counts, and showing appointments. Offers are submitted by buyers with an offer price and contingency type (NONE, FINANCING, INSPECTION, APPRAISAL). The offer price can exceed the listing price. If an offer has no contingency (NONE) and is submitted within 7 days of listing, the offer is flagged as high_priority. Transactions record the final sale price, closing costs (typically 2-5% of sale price), and closing date. Listing price for residential properties follows a log-normal distribution with log-mean 12.8 and log-variance 0.9. Days on market follows an exponential distribution with mean 28 days. Closing costs as percentage of sale price follow a normal distribution with mean 3.2% and standard deviation 0.6%.

A competitive gaming platform database. Games are developed by studios and published under different publishers. Players register accounts and accrue experience points. Player level follows a Zipfian distribution with exponent 1.8 (many low-level casual players, few high-level experts). Game sessions record start time, end time, score achieved, and the game mode (RANKED, CASUAL, TOURNAMENT). Session duration in minutes follows an exponential distribution with mean 45 minutes. Players earn achievements that are classified by rarity: COMMON 60%, UNCOMMON 25%, RARE 12%, LEGENDARY 3%. In-app purchases are made in a virtual currency; purchase amounts in USD follow a log-normal distribution with log-mean 1.5 and log-variance 0.8. If a player is under 13 years old, parental_consent_required must be true. If a purchase amount exceeds $50 in a single transaction, a verification flag must be set. Tournament scores must be non-negative integers. Expect 10M players, 500M game sessions, 100M purchases.

A food delivery platform database. Restaurants are categorized by cuisine type and have an average preparation time and a minimum order amount. Menu items have a price, calorie count, and dietary flags (vegetarian, vegan, gluten-free). Customer orders are placed with a selected restaurant, and each order has line items, a delivery address, and a total. Delivery drivers are assigned to orders and track pickup and delivery times. Order total follows a log-normal distribution with log-mean 3.4 and log-variance 0.45. Delivery time in minutes (from order placement to delivery completion) follows a normal distribution with mean 38 and standard deviation 11. Driver rating follows a normal distribution with mean 4.3 and standard deviation 0.4. If the order total is below $12.00, a delivery fee of at least $2.99 must be added. If the delivery time exceeds 60 minutes, a compensation_credit must be issued (compensation_credit > 0). Expect 50K restaurants, 5M customers, 20M orders.

A B2B SaaS platform billing and usage database. Organizations subscribe to plans with different feature tiers: FREE (up to 5 users), STARTER (up to 25 users), PROFESSIONAL (up to 100 users), ENTERPRISE (unlimited users). Monthly active users per organization follows a Poisson distribution with lambda 35. Feature usage events are recorded per user per day. If an organization is on the FREE plan, the active_user_count must not exceed 5. If the plan is STARTER and active_user_count exceeds 25, an automatic upgrade_prompt must be triggered. Invoices are generated monthly; invoice amounts follow a log-normal distribution with log-mean 7.2 and log-variance 1.1. Support tickets have priorities: LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH, CRITICAL. If a support ticket has CRITICAL priority, the resolution_hours must not exceed 4. Support resolution hours follow an exponential distribution with mean 18 hours. Expect 50K organizations, 2M users, 10M daily usage events.

A manufacturing supply chain database tracking suppliers, materials, purchase orders, and warehouse inventory. Suppliers have a reliability score (0.0 to 1.0) and a lead time in days that follows an exponential distribution with mean 12 days. Materials have a unit cost that follows a log-normal distribution with log-mean 2.8 and log-variance 1.2. Purchase orders have a status (DRAFT, SUBMITTED, CONFIRMED, IN_TRANSIT, RECEIVED, CANCELLED) and a total value. The received date must be NULL unless the status is RECEIVED. If a supplier's reliability score drops below 0.7, all new purchase orders from that supplier require dual_approval. Quality checks are performed on received shipments; a quality score below 0.85 requires a defect_report to be filed. Quality scores follow a normal distribution with mean 0.93 and standard deviation 0.06. Inventory quantity on hand must be non-negative. Expect 2K suppliers, 50K materials, 500K purchase orders per year.

An academic research publication database for a computer science conference management system. Authors are affiliated with institutions and have an h-index. Papers are submitted to venues (conferences or journals) and undergo peer review. Review scores range from 1 (strong reject) to 6 (strong accept) and follow a normal distribution with mean 3.8 and standard deviation 1.1. Citation counts per paper follow a Zipfian distribution with exponent 1.6 (most papers receive few citations, a small number become highly cited). If a paper receives an average review score below 3.0, its decision must be REJECTED. If the h-index of all authors on a paper is greater than 20 on average, the paper is flagged as high_profile. Keywords are tracked per paper with an importance weight (0.0 to 1.0). Papers with more than 50 pages are classified as full_paper = true. Expect 100K authors, 50K papers, 500K citation edges.

A clinical drug trial management database for a pharmaceutical company. Trials are categorized by phase (PHASE_1, PHASE_2, PHASE_3, PHASE_4) and have a protocol number, start date, and target enrollment count. Each trial recruits participants who undergo assessments at defined visit milestones. Primary efficacy scores are computed per participant visit and follow a normal distribution with mean 0.68 and standard deviation 0.14 (bounded 0 to 1). Adverse event severity follows a categorical distribution: Grade 1 (mild) 52%, Grade 2 (moderate) 30%, Grade 3 (severe) 13%, Grade 4 (life-threatening) 4%, Grade 5 (fatal) 1%. If an adverse event is Grade 4 or higher, the trial_safety_board_notified flag must be set to true. If the trial is Phase 3 and the primary efficacy score averaged across participants is below 0.55, the trial_status must be SUSPENDED or TERMINATED. Drug dosage in mg/kg follows a log-normal distribution with log-mean 1.8 and log-variance 0.5. Expect 500 trials, 50K participants, 500K adverse events.

A telecommunications call detail record (CDR) system. Subscribers belong to rate plans that define a monthly data cap in MB (modeled as a Poisson distribution with lambda 15000), a voice minutes allowance, and a billing cycle. CDRs capture every call and data session: calling party, called party, start timestamp, duration in seconds (non-negative), call type (VOICE, SMS, DATA, VIDEO_CALL), and a termination reason code. For DATA sessions, bytes uploaded and bytes downloaded must both be non-negative. Calls are routed through cell towers; tower coordinates (latitude -90 to 90, longitude -180 to 180) must be within valid bounds. Voice call duration in seconds follows an exponential distribution with mean 180 seconds. Data session bytes downloaded follows a log-normal distribution with log-mean 14.5 and log-variance 2.0. SMS messages have duration = 0. Roaming calls (tower country != subscriber country) must have a roaming_flag = true. Expect 10M subscribers, 300M CDRs per day.

A retail loyalty and rewards program database. Members earn points on purchases at partner stores. Tiers are BRONZE (0-999 points), SILVER (1000-4999 points), GOLD (5000-19999 points), PLATINUM (20000+ points). Point multiplier must be at least 1.5x for SILVER, 2.0x for GOLD, and 3.0x for PLATINUM. Member lifetime spend follows a log-normal distribution with log-mean 8.5 and log-variance 1.2. Points earned per transaction follows a Poisson distribution with lambda 45. If a member's lifetime spend exceeds $5000 and they are still SILVER tier, upgrade_eligible must be set to true. Redemptions convert points to discounts at a rate of 100 points = $1 discount. If a redemption would reduce a member's point balance below 0, the redemption must be rejected (is_valid = false). Bonus events multiply point earnings by a factor (1.5 to 5.0) during promotional periods. Expect 5M members, 50M transactions.

A professional football (soccer) league analytics database. Leagues contain multiple seasons, and each season has multiple teams competing. Players have a position (GOALKEEPER, DEFENDER, MIDFIELDER, FORWARD), a market value in EUR that follows a log-normal distribution with log-mean 13.8 and log-variance 1.5, and an age. Games record the home team, away team, date, and final score. Per-game player statistics include goals, assists, shots on target, passes completed, and minutes played. Goals scored per game follows a Poisson distribution with lambda 2.7 (total goals per match). Player market value must be non-negative. If a player's position is GOALKEEPER, their saves_per_game must be non-negative. Contracts specify salary per week in EUR (log-normal, log-mean 10.2, log-variance 1.0), contract start and end dates, and agent commission percentage (0-20%). Injuries track the type, the expected recovery days (exponential with mean 18 days), and whether the player is currently unavailable. Expect 50 teams, 1000 players, 500 games per season.

Okay so we basically run a mid-sized regional hospital -- about 400 beds -- and we need a database that tracks pretty much everything. Let me try to walk you through it. 

We have patients, obviously. Each patient has the usual stuff: name, date of birth, a national health ID of some kind, address, contact number, blood type (though sometimes we don't know it when they're first admitted, so that has to be optional), and their primary insurance provider. Some patients have secondary insurance too -- I guess we should track that somehow. A patient's age at admission is the thing that actually matters for some of our rules, not their current age, so maybe we store both or compute it, I'm not sure which is better. 

Providers -- that's doctors, nurses, residents, and other clinical staff. Each one has a license number, a specialty (for doctors anyway -- things like CARDIOLOGY, NEUROLOGY, ORTHOPEDICS, GENERAL_SURGERY, EMERGENCY_MEDICINE, INTERNAL_MEDICINE, PEDIATRICS, and probably others), and some kind of employment status. Residents are a bit different -- they're supervised by an attending physician, so there's a hierarchy there. I think we need to track which attending supervises which residents, but I'm not 100% sure how deep that needs to go. 

Patients come in through different pathways -- some walk in through the emergency department, some are referred from another doctor for an outpatient visit, and some get admitted as inpatients for a planned procedure or surgery. Each of these is kind of a different type of encounter I suppose. For inpatient stays we need to know which bed they're in, which ward, and their admission and discharge dates. A bed can only have one patient at a time, obviously. Ward capacity is something we track too -- each ward has a maximum number of beds and a current occupancy, though I realize that might be derivable rather than stored. 

During an encounter, providers place orders -- lab tests, medications, imaging studies, maybe procedures. I think each order has a status (like PENDING, IN_PROGRESS, COMPLETED, CANCELLED) and the provider who placed it. For lab orders, we need the result value and a reference range -- something like 'hemoglobin should be between 12 and 17' -- and a flag if the value is outside the normal range. Lab result values are going to vary by test type obviously, but in general I'd expect them to roughly follow a bell curve around the normal reference value, with standard deviation maybe 15-20% of the range. If a lab value is flagged as CRITICAL -- meaning dangerously outside the range -- the system must record that the ordering provider was notified. 

Medications: each prescription has a drug name, dosage, route of administration (ORAL, IV, IM, SUBCUTANEOUS, TOPICAL), frequency, start date, and end date. We need to track which formulary tier the drug belongs to -- I think our hospital has three tiers: generic, preferred brand, and non-preferred -- and payer contracts sometimes require prior authorization for non-preferred drugs. If prior authorization is required but not yet approved, the medication order should be flagged as PENDING_AUTH. 

Diagnoses are attached to encounters. We use ICD codes -- those standardized diagnosis codes, you know the ones -- and a description. A single encounter can have multiple diagnoses, and we want to distinguish the primary diagnosis from secondary ones. 

On the billing side, each encounter generates a claim. Claims go to a payer -- the patient's insurance company -- and have a billed amount, a contracted rate (which is what the payer actually agreed to pay), and the amount the patient owes after insurance pays. Billed amounts follow a log-normal distribution honestly, with a wide spread -- I'd guess log-mean around 8.5 and log-variance around 2.0. Claims can be SUBMITTED, PENDING, APPROVED, PARTIALLY_APPROVED, DENIED, or APPEALED. If a claim is denied more than twice by the same payer, it should automatically be escalated to our billing dispute team. 

We probably also need some kind of referral tracking -- when one doctor sends a patient to a specialist, there's usually a referral document. The referral has an urgency level (ROUTINE, URGENT, EMERGENT), and if it's EMERGENT the specialist must see the patient within 24 hours, which we'd want to track as a flag on the appointment. 

Scale-wise: maybe 200,000 patient records, 500,000 encounters per year, around 2 million orders annually. Lab result values are probably in the hundreds of thousands.

We're building a two-sided marketplace -- think of it as kind of a cross between Airbnb and Fiverr, where people can list either a physical space to rent OR a skilled service they offer, or honestly both. A host might rent out a workshop space and also offer woodworking lessons in it, you know? 

So hosts are people or businesses who list things. They have a profile, a payout bank account (or PayPal, we want to support a few methods), a verification status -- we check government ID and run some kind of background check, so there are different levels like UNVERIFIED, ID_VERIFIED, FULLY_VERIFIED -- and an average rating, though I guess that's computed, not stored. Guests are the people who book things. A person can be both a host and a guest, actually, we don't want to force separate accounts for that. 

Listings come in two flavors as I said: spaces and services. A space listing has an address, a type (STUDIO, OFFICE, WORKSHOP, OUTDOOR, VENUE, or OTHER), a maximum capacity in people, an hourly rate and/or a daily rate -- some hosts set both, some set only one -- and an availability calendar. The availability thing is a bit complicated: hosts can block out dates, and bookings also block dates, and we need to prevent double-booking. A service listing has a category (PHOTOGRAPHY, CATERING, CLEANING, TUTORING, FITNESS, LEGAL, CREATIVE, and probably other things we haven't thought of yet), a base price, and whether pricing is fixed or negotiable -- if negotiable, guests submit a proposed price and the host can accept or counter. 

Bookings are the core transaction. A booking ties a guest to a listing and has a start time, end time, the agreed price, a status (PENDING, CONFIRMED, ACTIVE, COMPLETED, CANCELLED_BY_GUEST, CANCELLED_BY_HOST, DISPUTED). When a booking is confirmed, we hold the payment -- we don't release it to the host until 24 hours after the booking completes or is marked complete by both parties, whichever comes first I think. If either party raises a dispute, the status flips to DISPUTED and it goes into a queue for our trust and safety team. 

Pricing is a bit nuanced. We take a platform commission -- 12% from the host payout and a 5% service fee on top of what the guest pays. So a guest actually pays 105% of the agreed price and the host receives 88%. For FULLY_VERIFIED hosts who have done more than 50 completed bookings, we reduce our commission to 8%. I'm not sure if we should encode that threshold logic directly in the database or handle it in application code, but you should probably know about it. 

Reviews work both ways: after a booking is completed, the guest can leave a review of the listing (1-5 stars, text comment), and the host can leave a review of the guest (also 1-5 stars). We're still debating whether reviews should be mutually anonymous until both parties have submitted them, kind of like Airbnb does it, but let's assume yes for now. Review scores should probably follow a left-skewed distribution -- most people rate 4 or 5, very few rate 1 or 2. A listing with fewer than 3 reviews shouldn't show an average rating publicly, just show 'New'. 

There's also a messaging system between hosts and guests. Messages belong to a conversation thread tied to a booking or a listing inquiry (before a booking exists). We probably want to flag messages that contain contact information like phone numbers or email addresses, to discourage off-platform communication. 

Cancellation policies: hosts choose a policy at the listing level -- FLEXIBLE (full refund up to 24 hours before), MODERATE (full refund up to 5 days before), STRICT (50% refund up to 7 days before, no refund after that). If a host cancels, the guest always gets a full refund plus a small credit, regardless of policy -- we want to disincentivize host cancellations. If the same host cancels more than 3 bookings in a 90-day window, they should be flagged for review. 

Scale: maybe 500,000 hosts, 5 million guests, 20 million listings, 10 million bookings per year. Review distribution skews heavily positive -- average rating probably around 4.3 out of 5 with standard deviation around 0.7.

We're building the back-end database for a retail brokerage platform -- think Robinhood or E*TRADE level, but we're starting with US equities and ETFs and plan to add options and fixed income later. Let me describe what we need to track. 

Users open accounts with us. An account has a type -- INDIVIDUAL, JOINT, IRA, ROTH_IRA, SEP_IRA, CUSTODIAL -- and a status (PENDING_APPROVAL, ACTIVE, RESTRICTED, SUSPENDED, CLOSED). For margin accounts (a subtype of individual or joint), there's a margin level and a buying power calculation which is roughly 2x the cash balance for standard margin, but it gets complicated with portfolio margin. Let's just say we need to track whether an account is cash or margin and what the current buying power is. An account must pass a KYC check before it becomes ACTIVE -- we store the KYC status and the date it was approved. 

Financial instruments: we need a master list of securities. Each has a ticker symbol, a name, an asset class (EQUITY, ETF, OPTION, BOND, MUTUAL_FUND), an exchange (NYSE, NASDAQ, AMEX, OTC), and for options we also need the underlying instrument, strike price, expiration date, and whether it's a call or a put. Options are a bit of a special case -- they derive their value from the underlying, so there's a parent-child relationship of sorts between the option and its underlying equity. 

Orders are placed by accounts. An order has a type: MARKET, LIMIT, STOP, STOP_LIMIT, TRAILING_STOP. It has a side (BUY or SELL), a quantity, a limit price if applicable, a stop price if applicable, a time in force (DAY, GTC meaning Good Till Cancelled, IOC meaning Immediate Or Cancel, FOK meaning Fill Or Kill), and a status (PENDING, OPEN, PARTIALLY_FILLED, FILLED, CANCELLED, REJECTED, EXPIRED). A MARKET order should never have a limit price set -- that's a validation rule we'd want to enforce. A LIMIT order must have a limit price. For a STOP_LIMIT order, both stop price and limit price are required. 

When an order gets executed, that creates one or more executions or fills -- because a large order might get filled in pieces at different prices. Each execution has an executed price, quantity, timestamp, and the exchange or venue it was routed to. The average fill price of all executions for a given order should equal the reported execution price on the order itself once fully filled -- I'm not sure if we store that redundantly or compute it. Commissions are zero for us (we're commission-free) but we do track regulatory fees -- SEC fee for sells and FINRA TAF for all trades -- these are tiny fractions of the trade value, like $0.000008 per dollar of sale proceeds. 

Positions track what each account currently holds. A position has an account, an instrument, a quantity, and an average cost basis -- which gets complicated when you buy multiple lots at different prices. Actually we might need to track individual lots separately for tax purposes (FIFO vs specific lot identification). I'm not sure how deep to go on that, let's at least track the lot-level cost basis. If an account holds a short position -- meaning they've sold shares they don't own -- the quantity is negative and they pay a stock borrow fee that varies by how hard-to-borrow the stock is. 

Settlement: US equity trades settle T+1 as of 2024 (it recently changed from T+2). The settlement record needs to track expected settlement date and actual settlement date -- sometimes they differ if there are fails. A failed settlement needs to be flagged and tracked. 

Market data: we need to store daily OHLCV (open, high, low, close, volume) for each instrument. Intraday we probably don't store in the main database, just the daily summary. Daily returns on equities roughly follow a normal distribution with mean near zero and standard deviation around 1.5-2.5% for individual stocks, much less for ETFs. 

Corporate actions: dividends, stock splits, mergers. For a dividend, we record the ex-date, record date, pay date, and amount per share. Cash dividends go into the account cash balance on the pay date. For a split (say 2-for-1), all positions and order quantities for the affected instrument need to be adjusted -- there should be some kind of adjustment log. 

Risk and compliance: if an account has made more than 3 day trades in a rolling 5-day window and the account balance is under $25,000, it triggers a Pattern Day Trader flag and the account gets restricted from placing further day trades. That's an actual FINRA rule, so it's non-negotiable. Also, short selling is not permitted in IRA accounts -- if someone tries to place a short sell order in an IRA account, the order must be REJECTED. 

Scale: around 2 million accounts, 10,000 instruments, 50 million orders per year, 100 million executions, 5 million daily OHLCV records (roughly 250 trading days times 20,000 instruments once we add options). Order quantities follow a power-law-ish distribution -- most orders are small (1-10 shares) but occasionally someone trades thousands of shares.
